title: You Were Never Supposed to Teach Alone Part 6 of 6
author: How to Teach With AI
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 24, 2026
summary: Closing out a six-part series, this piece argues that teaching was structurally set up as a one-person job even though it requires the range of tasks other knowledge professions split across whole teams of nurses, paralegals, or associates. It reframes AI tools not as features to chase but as four distinct "staff roles" a teacher can "hire": a Department Head that holds course voice and rubrics, Specialists for recurring tasks like rubric-writing and lesson planning, a Desktop Assistant for grading actual files, and a Senior Analyst that stress-tests lesson plans overnight. A weekly rhythm and 30-day rollout plan translate the metaphor into a habit, activating one new "staff member" per week rather than all four at once. The piece explicitly rejects framing this as a productivity hack, instead arguing the point is reclaiming personal time — sleep, family, side projects — that the profession has historically assumed teachers would sacrifice unpaid, and closes with a direct charge to "act like the boss" of the staff just built.
points: The piece argues teaching was structurally designed as a one-person job despite requiring the range of tasks other professions split across whole teams (nurses, paralegals, analysts).

It reframes AI tools as four distinct "staff roles" a teacher can "hire" — a Department Head for course voice/rubrics, Specialists for repeated tasks, a Desktop Assistant for grading, and a Senior Analyst for overnight lesson stress-testing.
A prescribed weekly rhythm and 30-day rollout plan is offered to convert the metaphor into a habit, one new "staff member" activated per week rather than all four at once.
The real payoff isn't framed as productivity but as reclaiming personal time — sleep, family, side projects — that the teaching profession has historically assumed teachers would sacrifice unpaid.
quotes: Every other knowledge profession has people. Doctors have nurses and medical techs and residents. Lawyers have paralegals and associates and researchers.
You were handed a job designed for four people and told to do it alone. You built a career around that lie.
You hired a Department Head. They hold your course, your voice, your rubrics, your standards. You stopped retyping your preamble into a chat window every Monday.
Do not chase features. Run your staff. Companies survive upgrades. Prompt libraries die every six months.

This is not about productivity. Be careful with that word. Productivity is what your dean wants from you. This is about reclaiming hours the profession stole from you when it decided teachers did not need a team.

You do not owe your institution your Sunday night. You do not owe your students a depleted version of yourself at 8am on Monday. You do not owe the profession the martyrdom it has been demanding of you for 40 years.

The difference between those two futures is not talent. It is not technical skill. It is not whether you are the AI person in your department. The difference is whether you act like the boss of the staff you just hired.
